meaning: A short summary of a paper or report, usually 150 to 250 words, that states the question, method and main finding.
A list of every source you consulted for a piece of work, including ones you did not cite directly.
A short note in the text that credits a source for an idea, quote or figure, pointing to its full entry in the reference list.
Presenting someone else's words, ideas or work as your own without crediting them.
To restate a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure, still crediting the source.
One or two sentences, usually at the end of the introduction, that state the main argument an essay will defend.
A testable prediction about what you expect to find, which an experiment or study is designed to support or refute.
The default claim that there is no effect or difference, which a statistical test tries to reject.
The probability of seeing results at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. A small value (often below 0.05) is taken as evidence against it.
The average: add the values up and divide by how many there are.
The middle value when the numbers are put in order; with an even count, the mean of the two middle ones.
The value that appears most often in a set.
A measure of how spread out values are around the mean. A small one means the values sit close to it.
The average of the squared distances from the mean; the square root of it is the standard deviation.
A measure of how two variables move together, from -1 to 1. It does not show that one causes the other.
A relationship where a change in one thing produces a change in another, which needs more evidence than correlation.
Describing data in words, themes and experiences rather than numbers, such as interviews or open comments.
Describing data as numbers that can be counted or measured, such as test scores or survey ratings.
Original evidence from the time or person you study, such as a diary, a dataset, an interview or a first report of an experiment.
A work that interprets or discusses primary sources, such as a textbook, a review article or a documentary.
Checking of a piece of research by independent experts in the field before it is published.
A survey of what has already been written on a topic, showing what is known, what is disputed and where the gaps are.
The overall approach and reasoning behind how a study was done, and why those methods suit the question.
The outline of a course: its topics, readings, assessments and dates.
Assessed work done during a course, such as essays, projects and labs, as opposed to a final exam.
Work that gives feedback to help you improve and usually does not count toward your final grade.
Work that measures what you have learned at the end of a unit and counts toward your final grade.
A marking grid that lists the criteria a piece of work is judged on and what each level of performance looks like.
The specific things a course says you should be able to do by the end of it.
A long piece of independent research written to complete a degree, usually at final-year or postgraduate level.
A spoken examination in which you answer questions about your own work, often for a dissertation or thesis.
A small class built around discussion, where students present and debate material instead of listening to a lecture.
A small-group or one-to-one session with a tutor, used to go through questions, problems or feedback.
Grade point average: the mean of your grades converted to points and weighted by credit.
A unit that measures the workload of a course. A degree needs a set number of credits to be awarded.
Extra time to hand in an assignment, granted for a reason such as illness or a documented need.
Postponing an exam or assessment to a later sitting, usually with an approved reason.
A final read for spelling, grammar, punctuation and formatting mistakes, after the content is settled.
An author-date style: cite (Author, year) in the text and list full details alphabetically at the end.
A referencing style from the American Psychological Association: author-date citations and a reference list, common in the social sciences.
A referencing style from the Modern Language Association: author-page citations and a works-cited list, common in the humanities.
A study method of working in focused 25-minute blocks separated by 5-minute breaks, with a longer break after four.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, such as after a day, then three days, then a week, which fixes it in memory better than cramming.
Testing yourself from memory instead of rereading, for example with flashcards or practice questions.
Learning by explaining an idea in plain words as if teaching a beginner, then going back to fill the gaps you found.
Mixing different topics or problem types in one study session rather than finishing one block at a time.
A memory aid, such as a rhyme or an acronym, that makes a list or fact easier to recall.
A diagram with a central idea in the middle and related ideas branching out from it.
A note-taking layout with a narrow cue column on the left, the notes on the right and a summary at the bottom.
Thinking about your own thinking: noticing what you understand, what you do not, and how you learn best.
Trying to learn a lot in a short time just before an exam; it works for the short term but is poor for lasting memory.
A finite, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or doing a calculation.
A named place in a program that holds a value which can change; in maths, a symbol that stands for an unknown or changing number.
When a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it, until a base case stops it.
A way to describe how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input gets larger, such as O(n) or O(n squared).
Application programming interface: a defined way for one program to ask another to do something or share data.
An organised collection of data stored so it can be searched, updated and kept consistent.
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a database table.
The rate at which a quantity changes: the slope of a function's graph at a point.
The accumulated total of a function over a range: the area under its graph.
A number from 0 to 1 that says how likely an event is; 0 is impossible and 1 is certain.
What you give up by choosing one option over the next best one.
The economic model in which price settles where the amount sellers offer equals the amount buyers want.
A general rise in prices over time, which lowers what a unit of money can buy.
Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services a country produces in a period.
The process by which plants, algae and some bacteria use light, water and carbon dioxide to make sugar and release oxygen.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical cells, used for growth and repair.
Cell division that produces four cells with half the usual chromosomes, used to make eggs and sperm.
The movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a weaker solution to a stronger one.
A measure of disorder or of how spread out energy is; in a closed system it tends to increase.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up by it.
The study of what is right and wrong, and the principles that guide a person's or a profession's conduct.
The branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is, how we get it and what justifies belief.
Based on observation or experiment rather than theory alone.
